Q: Why does case_when() in R work for one option with true and not work with another option? A:

First of all, you don't need to use case_when(). You can simply look for matching dates, and return the first one. This returns NA if there are no matches.

del1[grep(paste(c(dod1, dod2, dod3, dod4), collapse = "|"), del1)[1]]

#> [1] "Z:/addVI/sent_plusVI_Vermont_Chittenden_2024-08-27.tif"

But the reason this is happening is essentially the same as my answer to this post; case_when() requires all RHS values to have compatible lengths. When the LHS is any(...) it returns a single TRUE/FALSE, but the RHS del1[which(...)] returns character(0) (a length-0 vector) when which() finds no matches. In your first example, case_when() sees a length-0 RHS on the first branch and returns character(0) before even evaluating the second branch where the match exists.

This is why replacing the RHS with simple strings like "one", "two" worked as those are always length-1 regardless of what the LHS evaluates to.

Q: xpath select following node of a specific node A:

Use the following expression to select the first two wccontnetbox elements after the first wcheader1:

//table/tbody/tr[td[@class='wcheader1']][2]/
    following-sibling::tr[td[@class='wccontnetbox']][position()<3]/td

I'm using // because you don't show your full input. It would be better to use a direct path to the table (e.g. /html/body/<etc>/table...).

Use the following expression to select all nodes between the first and second wcheader1 elements:

//table/tbody/tr[td[@class='wcheader1']][1]/following-sibling::tr[
    count(.|//table/tbody/tr[td[@class='wcheader1']][2]/preceding-sibling::tr)
     =
    count(//table/tbody/tr[td[@class='wcheader1']][2]/
        preceding-sibling::tr)]/td[@class='wccontnetbox']

Note: This second expression uses the Kayessian node-set intersection formula. In general, use the following expression to find the intersection of $set1 and $set2:

$set1[count(.|$set2)=count($set2)]

Q: Why do C- and Fortran-ordered NumPy arrays show the same L1 cache-miss percentage when formatting a row? A:

The reason you don’t see them in perf stats is simply a signal-to-noise ratio issue.

Here’s what’s happening behind the scenes.

When you slice a[0] in F-contiguous order, you’re jumping 16,000 bytes in memory between each element. Since that easily crosses cache lines (and memory pages), fetching that row results in approximately 10,000 cache misses per loop. In contrast, when the elements are packed tightly together in C-contiguous order, you only get about 1,250 misses per loop. Over 1,000 iterations, the F-order script generates roughly 8.7 million more cache misses just from reading the array data.

So, why doesn’t perf show it?

The reason is due to the np.array2string function. Converting 10,000 floats to strings is an incredibly expensive CPU-bound operation. Python and NumPy perform complex algorithms to format the floats, allocate memory for millions of intermediate string objects, and join them all together. This process generates billions of L1 cache loads and tens of millions of baseline cache misses just by executing the interpreter and formatting overhead. Your 8.7 million extra data misses are essentially negligible compared to the noise caused by the string formatting. To actually benchmark it, you need to remove the string conversion overhead and use a fast, vectorized math operation like np.sum(). This forces the CPU to process the data much faster than it can fetch it from RAM.

import numpy as np
import sys

# Pass "C" or "F" as a command line argument
order = sys.argv[1]

N = 2000
a = np.ones((N, 5*N), dtype=np.float64, order=order)

# A tight loop that doesn't trigger string overhead
for _ in range(10000):
    x = np.sum(a[0])

If you run this for both C and F, you will finally see the massive, undeniable spike in L1-dcache-load-misses and execution time you were originally expecting!

Q: Can a bash script tell if it's being run via cron? A:

I needed to know if a script was run from a terminal, not by another script nor by cron.

After many tests, I ended up with this condition :

! ([ "$SHLVL" -gt "2" ] || [ -z "$TERM" ] || [ "$TERM" = "dumb" ])

which is true if and only if the script is run from a terminal.

Q: Powershell "You cannot run this script on the current system" A:

The error messages in your question imply that the actual command you ran must have been based on Install-PSResource rather than on the obsolescent Install-Module, namely something like:

# * May trigger a confirmation prompt.
# * Definitely looks for signatures and fails if the module isn't signed.
Install-PSResource -Name PrettyLs -AuthenticodeCheck

To fix your problems:

  • add the -TrustRepository switch, which bypasses the installation confirmation prompt.

    • Note: This switch only takes effect for the call at hand; to avoid having to re-specify -TrustRepository for every call, make a one-time call to Set-PSResourceRepository with the name of the repository of interest and the -Trusted switch; e.g., to persistently trust the PSGallery repository:

      Set-PSResourceRepository -Name PSGallery -Trusted

  • omit the -AuthenticodeCheck switch, which causes installation of a given module to fail if it isn't signed, which is what you saw with the third-party PrettyLs module.

Thus:

# * Presents NO confirmation prompt, due to -TrustRepository
#   To trust the PSGallery repo persistently, run:
#      Set-PSResourceRepository PSGallery -Trusted
# * Performs NO signature verification (due to absence of -AuthenticodeCheck)
Install-PSResource -Name PrettyLs -TrustRepository

Also note:

  • The currently effective execution policy is irrelevant when installing modules with Install-PSResource (or Install-Module); it only matters when it comes to using (importing) them.

    • Since you've set your effective (current-user) policy to Unrestricted, you shouldn't have any problem importing unsigned modules installed via Install-PSResource.

    • This would also apply if you used the RemoteSigned policy, which is generally the safer choice.

  • Install-PSResource - unlike Install-Module - has no -AllowClobber switch; instead, its logic is inverted: its -NoClobber switch prevents installation of modules containing commands whose names conflict with existing commands.

    • That said, neither switch is called for in your case, at least with respect to built-in commands: the PrettyLs module's only exported command is an ls function, which doesn't clash with the built-in ls alias on Windows, and also not with the external executable /bin/ls on Unix-like platforms (in PowerShell (Core) 7)

  • The above also implies the following with respect to calling the custom ls function:

    • To predictably invoke it (rather than the alias on Windows / the external executable on Unix), call it as PrettyLs\ls, i.e. prefix it with the module name.

    • To be able to call it as ls only:

      • On Windows: First run Remove-Item Alias:ls to remove the built-in alias (aliases have higher command precedence than functions).

      • On Unix-like platforms: First run Import-Module PrettyLs i.e. explicitly import the module (e.g. via your $PROFILE file), so that PowerShell loads the function and therefore makes it take precedence over the external ls executable.
